planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer.

directions: Beurre Clairgeau was raised near Nantes, France by nurseryman Pierre Clairgeau around 1830 and quickly became famous across Europe and North America for its enormous, strikingly bronze-red russeted fruit. The tree is vigorous and reliably heavy-cropping, producing pears valued historically more for their dramatic size and color at fruit shows than for top dessert quality, though well-ripened fruit is juicy and pleasantly sweet. Plant it in deep, well-drained soil with a compatible pollinizer, since it is only partially self-fertile. Pick while still firm in early to mid fall and finish ripening indoors for the best eating texture.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer.

directions: Belle Lucrative was bred in Belgium by the pioneering pomologist Jean-Baptiste Van Mons in the early nineteenth century and is sometimes listed under the closely related name Fondante d'Automne. It ripens in early autumn, producing medium-sized, smooth-skinned pears whose melting, sweet, finely textured flesh made it one of the most highly regarded dessert pears of the Victorian era. The tree bears reliably once established but benefits from a compatible pollinizer and a sheltered site. Harvest while the fruit is still firm, then let it finish ripening indoors for a few days for the best flavor.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer.

directions: Triomphe de Vienne was introduced by the Croux nursery of Vienne, France in the 1870s and became a widely planted commercial dessert pear across continental Europe. Its large, conical fruit ripens in late summer to early fall with juicy, sweet, slightly musky flesh under yellow skin blushed with red. The tree grows vigorously and crops heavily once established, making it a dependable choice for a home orchard with a compatible pollinizer nearby. Pick the fruit while still firm and ripen it indoors at room temperature for the best texture.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer.

directions: Doyenne Boussoch originated in Belgium in the early nineteenth century, reputedly raised by a grower named Boussoch near Mons, and was widely distributed by European and American nurseries through the 1800s as a reliable early-autumn dessert pear. The fruit is large, with yellow skin often washed with red and crisp, juicy, moderately sweet flesh that ripens relatively quickly after picking. It is a vigorous, productive tree best grown with a compatible pollinizer in full sun and well-drained soil. Pick while firm in late summer and ripen indoors for just a few days, since the fruit does not hold long once mature.
sources: Downing, Fruits and Fruit Trees of America (historical reference)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer.

directions: Beurre d'Amanlis takes its name from the Brittany village of Amanlis in France, where it was discovered in the early nineteenth century, and was prized as one of the earliest-ripening of the classic buttery Beurre-type pears. Its large, somewhat irregular fruit has thin greenish-yellow skin and very juicy, melting flesh with a mild sweet flavor, best eaten soon after ripening since it does not store well. The tree is vigorous and bears early and heavily, making it a popular choice for nineteenth-century market orchards. Harvest in late summer while still firm and finish ripening indoors for just a few days before the fruit turns soft.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer.

directions: Citron des Carmes, also known in France as Madeleine, is among the oldest named pear varieties still documented, traced to Carmelite monastery orchards near Paris as early as the sixteenth century. It is valued chiefly as one of the very first pears to ripen each year, bearing small to medium lemon-yellow fruit with soft, juicy, mildly sweet flesh that spoils quickly and must be eaten within a few days of picking. The tree is moderately vigorous and adapted to a wide range of soils, making it a historically popular choice for early summer harvest before other pears come into season. Pick as soon as the fruit yields slightly to gentle pressure, since it does not improve with extended storage.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in a warm, sheltered, well-drained site with a compatible pollinizer.

directions: Gansel's Bergamot is an old English dessert pear dating to the eighteenth century, traditionally said to be named for a General Gansel who first distributed it. Like other bergamot-type pears it is rounded and somewhat flattened rather than the typical pear shape, with heavily russeted skin and dense, richly flavored, aromatic flesh considered superior to many other bergamots of its era. It ripens in late summer on a moderately vigorous tree that benefits from a warm, sheltered position and a compatible pollinizer. Harvest while firm and allow a short ripening period indoors to develop its full sweetness.

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees on vigorous rootstock in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; allow ample room for this large, long-lived cooking pear.

directions: Uvedale's St Germain, also recorded historically as Uvedale's Warden, is an old English culinary pear documented since at least the seventeenth century and traditionally grown for baking and stewing rather than fresh eating. The fruit is unusually large and hard even when mature, with coarse, firm flesh that only becomes palatable after long cooking, which made it a staple of traditional warden pies and preserves. The tree itself grows exceptionally large and long-lived compared with most dessert pears, so it needs ample room and patience before it begins to crop. Harvest in late fall after the fruit has fully colored, since unlike dessert pears it is picked hard and stores well into winter for cooking.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer.

directions: Swan's Egg is a small, old English dessert pear documented in nineteenth-century pomological manuals, named for its compact, smoothly egg-shaped fruit. The thin greenish-russet skin covers sweet, melting flesh that, while not large or showy, was valued in cottage gardens and traditional orchards for its reliable cropping and pleasant flavor. The tree is modestly vigorous and well suited to smaller garden spaces compared with many other heirloom European pears. Pick in early to mid fall while still firm and ripen indoors for a few days before eating.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer.

directions: Koonce is an American heirloom pear that originated in Illinois and has long been recommended by home orchard and extension programs for its unusually early, precocious bearing and good resistance to fire blight. The medium-sized fruit ripens in midsummer, well ahead of Bartlett, with soft, juicy, mildly sweet flesh best used fresh since it does not keep long. The tree begins fruiting at a young age and tolerates the humid growing conditions of the eastern and midwestern United States better than many European pears. Harvest as soon as the fruit begins to soften and color, since it passes its prime quickly on the tree.

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in early spring once soil can be worked, in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible cold-hardy pollinizer.

directions: Patten was introduced by Charles G. Patten, a pioneering fruit breeder of Charles City, Iowa, who worked in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries to develop tree fruits able to survive winters far colder than most European pears tolerate. It produces medium-sized, juicy fruit of modest dessert quality, but its real value has always been its exceptional cold hardiness, allowing gardeners well north of the usual pear range to grow it successfully. The tree is moderately vigorous and benefits from a compatible cold-hardy pollinizer such as Golden Spice or Luscious planted nearby. Pick in early fall while firm and ripen indoors for the best texture.
sources: Iowa State University horticulture extension reference

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in early spring once soil can be worked, in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible cold-hardy pollinizer.

directions: Parker was released by the University of Minnesota fruit breeding program in 1934 as part of an effort to extend pear growing into climates far too cold for standard European dessert pears. It bears medium-sized, sweet, juicy fruit with flavor and texture generally considered better than many other extreme-hardy pears of its era, ripening in early fall. The tree is reliably productive and benefits from a compatible pollinizer such as another cold-hardy selection like Luscious or Golden Spice. Harvest while still firm and allow the fruit to finish ripening indoors for the best eating quality.
sources: University of Minnesota horticulture extension reference
